(This afternoon through next Friday)

WEATHER PATTERN OVERVIEW: Currently, we are sitting around the 40s 
to 50s in most of the CWA, with a few bands of clouds extending 
most of the watch area. At this time, it is important to shout-out
this trough currently sitting over the Pacific Coast states which
will very soon become the key to our forecast as we proceed 
through the weekend. As we move through today, the sfc low to our 
west will start pushing up on the ridge to our east, with the cold
front over California beginning to create strong compression in 
the surface pressure gradient, giving us strong gusty winds, which
is the biggest highlight we have at this time. There is currently
a wind advisory in effect for the entire CWA, with potential for 
wind gusts in the valleys to reach the mid 30s to low 40s, and 
potential for gusts in the lower 50s along the mountain passes 
today. This will create possible impacts in blowing dust reducing
visibility, and high profile vehicles may find travel difficult. Winds
for the most part are going to be southerly until the front 
passes through tonight (around 8-10pm- ish for the western- most 
parts of the area, and 8-10am- ish for the eastern- most parts of 
the area), calming them down (unlike the child on my flight back)
and bringing a generally northerly flow. Along this front, we are
expecting to see some weak instability and broad moisture 
advection off of the Pacific Coast. With the potential for lift on
isolated shortwaves ahead of the front, and general synoptic 
lifting along the front, it can be expected that scattered showers
will present themselves across the CWA, with potential for 
mountain snow in the higher elevations later this evening, 
especially in the southern regions. Long story short, to quote 
Ollie Williams, “It’s Gon’ Rain!” Rainfall rates themselves should
remain relatively low, but our 6 hour QPF values ranging from 
0.05-0.6”. Higher instability will be present in parts of White 
Pine, and northern Nye counties, so some isolated thunderstorms do
pose a slight risk for higher localized rainfall rates, but the 
models are currently keeping rainfall rates generally below 
0.2”/hour. In terms of snowfall, the highest mountain peaks could 
be expecting up to 6” of snow, with the lower mountain passes 
spitting out T-2” of snowfall. The NBM is going to keep the snow- 
level around 8,000’ this morning, lowering to about 6,500’ tonight
ahead of the front, so unfortunately not quite to the valleys 
before the precipitation starts clearing out of the region around 
the midnight to 3ish hours for the eastern half of the CWA, 
9-10pm-ish hours for the western half. 

Looking at the temperatures, it is time to start breaking out 
those jackets as we will begin to see a major cooling trend 
overall. Highs for today will be sitting around the mid 40s to the
upper 50s, with a nearly uniform set of lows in the mid 30s. As 
we push the weekend, passed the cold front, highs will see a peak 
slightly warmer than today in tomorrows drier airmass, before 
general cooling starting in the upper 40s/ low 50s, and eventually
decreasing to the mid 20s to 30s by the end of next week, but 
that is still far out, so specifics still have relatively low 
confidence. 

Fast forwarding to early next week, another storm system will 
approach our later from the Pacific with a strong trough. This 
area of low-pressure will bring another round of precipitation to 
our area Monday into Tuesday time-frame. As it stands now, this 
second system will have slightly cooler air and more moisture to 
work with than the first one, so it could pack more of a punch. 
Diving into more specifics, the odds of seeing 1+ inch of snow are
pretty high across the higher elevations and some of the summits.
At this time, most of the lower elevation areas may miss out on 
the impactful snow chances (greater than 1 inch), but model 
guidance is suggesting that minor snow accumulations may still 
occur. In addition, rainfall amounts will likely be higher than 
the first system. NBM guidance suggest rainfall amounts around a 
half-inch or greater across the entire CWA with this secondary 
system. Like with the first system, this system will also be a 
quick hitter, so not expecting any flooding issues at this time. 
Tuesday afternoon could once again be breezy, with wind gusts 
between 15-30mph across the area.

As we look even further into the week, another system may impact 
the area late Wednesday and beyond. This system is projected to be
the coldest of the 3. In fact, it is even possible that the 
higher elevations of the CWA may not even get above freezing for a
few days in this time frame. It is way too early to dive into 
specifics as we are 5+ days out, but as it stands now, this system
will have the greatest shot of producing snow across the entire 
CWA, even the chance of impactful snow all the way to the valleys.
We will continue to reevaluate the forecast over the next few 
days,
